item.title: [Ep.20] Managing ACM Policies with OpenShift GitOps
item.dc:creator: Articles by Thomas Jungbauer
item.description: Policies as code: let OpenShift GitOps deploy Advanced Cluster Management policies from Git, generate them with the PolicyGenerator, use hub templates for per-cluster values and bootstrap Argo CD on every new cluster with a policy.
item.content:encoded:
In [Ep.18] I recommended ACM policies for the audited baseline of a cluster and Argo CD for everything that needs rendering. [Ep.19] showed how ACM feeds Argo CD with clusters and the different models that can be used in Argo CD. This part turns the integration around: Argo CD deploys ACM policies, and a policy bootstraps Argo CD on every new cluster.

The result is a setup where the policies live in Git, are reviewed in pull requests like any other change, and ACM does what it is good at: distribution, enforcement and compliance reporting.

The topic turned out to be too big for a single article, so I have split it into multiple parts and maybe I should have split into even more. This is the third:

  1. [Ep.18] OpenShift GitOps or Advanced Cluster Management? Choosing the right tool What each tool does, where they overlap and a decision guide.

  2. [Ep.19] ACM and OpenShift GitOps: push, pull and the Argo CD Agent: how ACM registers clusters in Argo CD, and how to set up each of the three delivery models.

  3. [Ep.20] Managing ACM Policies with OpenShift GitOps (this article): policies as code, the PolicyGenerator, hub templates and bootstrapping Argo CD with a policy.

Everything in this series was written against OpenShift GitOps 1.22 (Argo CD 3.5) and Advanced Cluster Management 2.17 (Open Cluster Management). Technology Preview and GA states move quickly in both products, so check the release notes of your versions before you commit to a design.
While I am using the term "Advanced Cluster Management" in this article, I am referring to the product formerly known as Open Cluster Management. Same counts for Argo CD and OpenShift GitOps.

Three integration patterns

There are three ways to combine policies and Argo CD. They are not exclusive, most mature setups combine the first two.

Pattern How it works Strength Weakness

A: Argo CD deploys policies

Policies live in Git, generated by the PolicyGenerator. The hub Argo CD syncs them to the hub, ACM propagates and evaluates them.

Policy as code with review, compliance dashboard in ACM

Needs the PolicyGenerator plugin in Argo CD

B: A policy bootstraps Argo CD

One enforced policy installs OpenShift GitOps and a root Application on every placed cluster. From there, Argo CD takes over.

New clusters configure themselves on import

The bootstrap needs proper planning and automation.

C: Policies configure directly

ConfigurationPolicies apply the cluster configuration themselves. No Argo CD on the spokes.

One tool, compliance built in

Weaker diff and ordering, large YAML in policies

Pattern C is fine for small, compliance-driven setups. For everything else I recommend A for governance and B for the fleet bootstrap. The rest of this article shows both.

Whatever option you choose, one rule from Ep.18 still applies: one owner per object. If Argo CD manages an object, a policy may only look at it in inform mode.

Preparing the hub Argo CD

You need an Argo CD instance on the hub that can sync to the hub itself. That instance needs three things before it can deploy policies:

  1. permissions for the policy API,

  2. the PolicyGenerator plugin,

  3. optionally, health checks for policies.

A second Argo CD instance for the hub

In Ep.19, the default instance openshift-gitops became the principal of the Argo CD Agent. Its application-controller is disabled, so it cannot sync anything to the hub itself, and the manifests of agent Applications are rendered on the managed clusters anyway. The policies, however, must be created on the hub.

This article therefore uses a second, small Argo CD instance on the hub that only takes care of the hub configuration: policy-gitops in the namespace of the same name. If your default instance still has its application-controller (push or pull model), you can use it instead. Replace policy-gitops with openshift-gitops in the examples below.

Second Argo CD instance for the hub configuration
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: policy-gitops
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1beta1
kind: ArgoCD
metadata:
  name: policy-gitops (1)
  namespace: policy-gitops
spec: {} (2)
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: acm-policies
  labels:
    argocd.argoproj.io/managed-by: policy-gitops (3)
1 The service account of the application-controller is named after the instance: policy-gitops-argocd-application-controller.
2 The PolicyGenerator plugin is added in the next sections.
3 policy-gitops is a namespace-scoped instance. The label allows it to manage the namespace acm-policies, where the policies live. The namespace must exist before the first sync, because the instance cannot create namespaces itself.

Permissions

The application-controller of the instance cannot create policies and Placements. Create a ClusterRole and bind it to the controller’s service account:

Not required if Argo CD runs as cluster-admin.
ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding for the hub Argo CD
kind: ClusterRole
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: openshift-gitops-policy-admin
rules:
  - apiGroups:
      - policy.open-cluster-management.io
    resources:
      - policies
      - configurationpolicies
      - certificatepolicies
      - operatorpolicies
      - policysets
      - placementbindings
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
  - apiGroups:
      - cluster.open-cluster-management.io
    resources:
      - placements
      - placements/status
      - placementdecisions
      - placementdecisions/status
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
---
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: policy-gitops-policy-admin
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: policy-gitops-argocd-application-controller
    namespace: policy-gitops
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: openshift-gitops-policy-admin

The ClusterRole in the ACM documentation also contains placementrules. I left them out on purpose: PlacementRules are deprecated.

The PolicyGenerator plugin

Creating the policy YAML by hand is tough and error-prone. Every manifest has to be wrapped in a ConfigurationPolicy, which is wrapped in a Policy, which needs a Placement and a PlacementBinding. The PolicyGenerator solves this. It is a Kustomize generator plugin that takes plain manifests and wraps them for you.

The plugin is not part of the OpenShift GitOps images. An init container copies it from an ACM image into the repo-server, and Kustomize must be allowed to run alpha plugins.

The setup is described in the ACM documentation: ACM 2.17: Accessing the Policy Generator from OpenShift GitOps.

ArgoCD resource on the hub with the PolicyGenerator plugin (excerpt)
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1beta1
kind: ArgoCD
metadata:
  name: policy-gitops
  namespace: policy-gitops
spec:
  kustomizeBuildOptions: --enable-alpha-plugins (1)
  repo:
    env:
      - name: KUSTOMIZE_PLUGIN_HOME
        value: /etc/kustomize/plugin
    initContainers:
      - name: policy-generator-install
        image: registry.redhat.io/rhacm2/multicluster-operators-subscription-rhel9:v2.17 (2)
        command:
          - /bin/bash
        args:
          - -c
          - cp /policy-generator/PolicyGenerator-not-fips-compliant /policy-generator-tmp/PolicyGenerator (3)
        volumeMounts:
          - mountPath: /policy-generator-tmp
            name: policy-generator
    volumeMounts:
      - mountPath: /etc/kustomize/plugin/policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1/policygenerator
        name: policy-generator
    volumes:
      - name: policy-generator
        emptyDir: {}
1 Allows Kustomize to execute the generator plugin.
2 The tag must match the minor version of your ACM hub (oc get multiclusterhub -n open-cluster-management -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.currentVersion}'). Update it after every hub upgrade, or let a policy do it (see Keeping the image tag in sync).
3 Copies the plugin from the image to the plugin directory.

If your policy folders contain Helm charts that should be rendered before the policies are generated, add the environment variable POLICY_GEN_ENABLE_HELM with the value "true" to spec.repo.env.

Keeping the image tag in sync

A fixed tag has one weakness: after a hub upgrade, the PolicyGenerator in the repo-server is still the old one until somebody updates the tag. The ACM documentation provides an example of a policy that keeps the image tag in sync. After an upgrade of the hub, the policy changes the image of the init container automatically.

The policy runs on the hub only, so it needs a Placement for local-cluster. The hub carries the label local-cluster=true, and it is part of the cluster set global, which must be bound to the policy namespace:

Policy that keeps the PolicyGenerator image in sync with the hub
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta2
kind: ManagedClusterSetBinding
metadata:
  name: global
  namespace: acm-policies
spec:
  clusterSet: global (1)
---
apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: Policy
metadata:
  name: argocd-policy-generator
  namespace: acm-policies
  annotations:
    policy.open-cluster-management.io/standards: NIST SP 800-53
    policy.open-cluster-management.io/categories: CM Configuration Management
    policy.open-cluster-management.io/controls: CM-2 Baseline Configuration
spec:
  remediationAction: enforce (2)
  disabled: false
  policy-templates:
    - objectDefinition:
        apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
        kind: ConfigurationPolicy
        metadata:
          name: argocd-policy-generator
        spec:
          severity: medium
          object-templates:
            - complianceType: musthave
              objectDefinition:
                apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1beta1
                kind: ArgoCD
                metadata:
                  name: policy-gitops
                  namespace: policy-gitops
                spec:
                  kustomizeBuildOptions: --enable-alpha-plugins
                  repo:
                    env:
                      - name: KUSTOMIZE_PLUGIN_HOME
                        value: /etc/kustomize/plugin
                    initContainers:
                      - name: policy-generator-install
                        image: '{{ (index (lookup "apps/v1" "Deployment" "open-cluster-management" "multicluster-operators-hub-subscription").spec.template.spec.containers 0).image }}' (3)
                        command:
                          - /bin/bash
                        args:
                          - -c
                          - cp /policy-generator/PolicyGenerator-not-fips-compliant /policy-generator-tmp/PolicyGenerator
                        volumeMounts:
                          - mountPath: /policy-generator-tmp
                            name: policy-generator
                    volumeMounts:
                      - mountPath: /etc/kustomize/plugin/policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1/policygenerator
                        name: policy-generator
                    volumes:
                      - name: policy-generator
                        emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta1
kind: Placement
metadata:
  name: hub-only
  namespace: acm-policies
spec:
  clusterSets:
    - global
  predicates:
    - requiredClusterSelector:
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            local-cluster: "true" (4)
---
apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: PlacementBinding
metadata:
  name: argocd-policy-generator
  namespace: acm-policies
placementRef:
  apiGroup: cluster.open-cluster-management.io
  kind: Placement
  name: hub-only
subjects:
  - apiGroup: policy.open-cluster-management.io
    kind: Policy
    name: argocd-policy-generator
1 The cluster set global contains every managed cluster, including the hub. The Placement below narrows it down to the hub. Creating a ManagedClusterSetBinding requires the permissions managedclustersetbindings and managedclustersets/bind, which are not part of the ClusterRole above. Create it once as cluster administrator, or extend the ClusterRole if Argo CD shall sync it.
2 We enforce this policy.
3 lookup reads the deployment of the ACM subscription controller, and the template takes the image of its first container. That is exactly the image the init container needs, in the version of the running hub.
4 ACM sets this label on the hub’s own ManagedCluster.

Two things to keep in mind:

  • Write this policy as plain YAML, not as PolicyGenerator input. It installs the generator, so it cannot depend on it (hen-egg problem). Argo CD can sync it from Git without the plugin.

  • One owner per object. The policy now manages the plugin part of the ArgoCD resource policy-gitops. If that resource is also deployed by Argo CD (for example, from a Helm chart for OpenShift GitOps), remove the plugin settings from there, or the two will overwrite each other.

Policy health in Argo CD

By default, Argo CD considers a policy healthy as soon as it exists. That is not very useful: you want to see in Argo CD whether the policy is compliant. The policy collection of the Open Cluster Management project contains a policy that adds the matching health checks (resourceHealthChecks) to the ArgoCD resource: argocd-policy-healthchecks.yaml. The policy adds the health checks to every ArgoCD instance it finds on the cluster, so policy-gitops is covered as well. It is shipped with remediationAction: inform: set it to enforce, otherwise it only reports the missing health checks. After that, Argo CD shows a non-compliant policy as Degraded.

Pattern A: policies as code

Pattern A is the governance part of the integration: the policies live in Git, Argo CD on the hub brings them into the cluster, and ACM does the rest. You never create a policy in the ACM console or with oc apply again. Every change is a pull request, and the history of your compliance is stored in Git.

The example in this section builds two policies that show both sides of a policy:

  • service-mesh installs Red Hat OpenShift Service Mesh 3 on the selected clusters: the Operator and a control plane. It is enforced and the manifests are applied in a fixed order, because the control plane resources can only be created after the Operator has installed its CRDs.

  • no-kubeadmin checks that the kubeadmin secret does not exist anymore. It only informs: ACM reports every cluster where the secret is still present, but nothing is deleted automatically.

Both start as plain Kubernetes manifests in Git. The PolicyGenerator wraps them into Policy, Placement and PlacementBinding, so you do not have to write the policy structure yourself.

This requires the hub Argo CD instance policy-gitops with the PolicyGenerator plugin, as described in the previous section.

The following diagram shows the complete flow, from Git to the compliance status in ACM and Argo CD:

Policies as code: from plain manifests in Git to compliance on every cluster

What happens under the hood:

  1. The hub Argo CD renders the policies from Git and syncs them to the hub.

  2. The result is a set of Policy, Placement and PlacementBinding objects in the namespace acm-policies.

  3. ACM creates a replicated policy in the namespace of every selected cluster on the hub.

  4. The policy framework on each managed cluster pulls its replicated policy, evaluates it and, in enforce mode, fixes what is different.

  5. The compliance status flows back to the hub and shows up in the ACM governance view, per policy and cluster.

  6. With the policy health checks, Argo CD shows a non-compliant policy as Degraded.

Repository layout

acm-policies/
├── kustomization.yaml
├── policy-generator.yaml
└── input
    ├── service-mesh
    │   ├── 01-subscription.yaml       # OpenShift Service Mesh 3 Operator
    │   ├── 02-namespace-istio-system.yaml
    │   ├── 03-namespace-istio-cni.yaml
    │   ├── 04-istiocni.yaml           # CNI plugin, required on OpenShift
    │   └── 05-istio.yaml              # the control plane
    └── no-kubeadmin
        └── kubeadmin-secret.yaml

The files in input/ are plain Kubernetes manifests, exactly as you would apply them with oc apply. The Operator is installed in the namespace openshift-operators, which already has an OperatorGroup for all namespaces, so neither a namespace nor an OperatorGroup is needed for it:

input/service-mesh/01-subscription.yaml
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1alpha1
kind: Subscription
metadata:
  name: servicemeshoperator3
  namespace: openshift-operators
spec:
  channel: stable-3.4 (1)
  installPlanApproval: Automatic
  name: servicemeshoperator3
  source: redhat-operators
  sourceNamespace: openshift-marketplace
1 Pins the minor version. Use stable to always get the latest version.

The control plane consists of two cluster-scoped resources, IstioCNI and Istio, each pointing to its own namespace (istio-cni and istio-system):

input/service-mesh/04-istiocni.yaml
apiVersion: sailoperator.io/v1
kind: IstioCNI
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  namespace: istio-cni
input/service-mesh/05-istio.yaml
apiVersion: sailoperator.io/v1
kind: Istio
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  namespace: istio-system

And the kubeadmin secret that must not exist:

if your original kubeadmin secret is still present, you can ignore this yaml. Honestly, I am not even sure if this would work, once you have removed the secret.
input/no-kubeadmin/kubeadmin-secret.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: kubeadmin
  namespace: kube-system

The kustomization.yaml only references the generator:

kustomization.yaml
generators:
  - policy-generator.yaml

Render the folder locally before you push. If it does not render on your machine, it will not render in Argo CD either. With the PolicyGenerator binary in your Kustomize plugin path:

kustomize build --enable-alpha-plugins acm-policies/

The output contains a Policy, a Placement and a PlacementBinding per policy.

The PolicyGenerator configuration

The file policy-generator.yaml is the heart of the setup. It does not contain any policy itself, it only describes which policies the generator shall create from the manifests in input/. It has two parts:

  • policyDefaults apply to every policy: the namespace on the hub where the policies are created, the default remediation action and severity, and the Placement that decides which clusters receive them.

  • policies lists the policies, each with its name, the manifests it contains and the settings that differ from the defaults.

For every entry in policies, the generator creates a Policy, a Placement and a PlacementBinding. The manifests are wrapped into a ConfigurationPolicy inside the Policy: by default all manifests of a policy into one, with consolidateManifests: false one per manifest. Our two policies use this as follows: service-mesh overrides the defaults to enforce and to apply its manifests in order, while no-kubeadmin keeps the defaults and only changes the compliance type.

policy-generator.yaml
apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: PolicyGenerator
metadata:
  name: cluster-baseline
policyDefaults:
  namespace: acm-policies
  remediationAction: inform (1)
  severity: medium
  placement:
    labelSelector:
      matchExpressions:
        - key: name (5)
          operator: In
          values:
            - sno
            - bm
policies:
  - name: service-mesh
    remediationAction: enforce (2)
    orderManifests: true (3)
    consolidateManifests: false
    manifests:
      - path: input/service-mesh/01-subscription.yaml
      - path: input/service-mesh/02-namespace-istio-system.yaml
      - path: input/service-mesh/03-namespace-istio-cni.yaml
      - path: input/service-mesh/04-istiocni.yaml
      - path: input/service-mesh/05-istio.yaml
  - name: no-kubeadmin
    manifests:
      - path: input/no-kubeadmin/
        complianceType: mustnothave (4)
1 Default for all policies: report only.
2 This policy is enforced.
3 Creates one ConfigurationPolicy per manifest and makes each one depend on the previous one: first the Subscription, then the namespaces, then IstioCNI and Istio. Note that the Subscription policy is compliant as soon as the Subscription exists, not when the Operator is installed. Until the CRDs are there, the IstioCNI policy reports an error and is evaluated again. If you want to wait for the installed Operator, use an OperatorPolicy instead of the Subscription, as shown in Pattern B.
4 The kubeadmin secret must not exist. In inform mode, ACM reports every cluster where it still exists. Remove it with care, only after an identity provider is configured.
5 Selects the clusters sno and bm. ACM sets the label name on every ManagedCluster. For a growing fleet, a label such as environment=production or the cluster set label cluster.open-cluster-management.io/clusterset scales better than a list of names.

Bind the cluster sets to the policy namespace

A Placement only sees the clusters of cluster sets that are bound to its own namespace. The bindings from Ep.19 live in openshift-gitops, so the Placements in acm-policies would find no cluster at all. ACM then shows the warning "ClusterSets failed to load. Verify that there is at least one ClusterSet bound to your selected namespace."

Bind the cluster set production to acm-policies, and global as well if you use the policy that keeps the PolicyGenerator image in sync (its Placement selects the hub from global):

ManagedClusterSetBindings in the policy namespace
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta2
kind: ManagedClusterSetBinding
metadata:
  name: production
  namespace: acm-policies
spec:
  clusterSet: production
---
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta2
kind: ManagedClusterSetBinding
metadata:
  name: global
  namespace: acm-policies
spec:
  clusterSet: global

The generated Placements select sno and bm by name, from the cluster sets bound to acm-policies. Check the result:

oc get placementdecisions -n acm-policies \
  -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CLUSTERS:.status.decisions[*].clusterName

The Argo CD Application

On the hub, one Application syncs the folder:

Application for the policies
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: acm-policies
  namespace: policy-gitops (1)
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/tjungbauer/acm-policies.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: .
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: acm-policies
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
1 The Application belongs to the instance policy-gitops. No CreateNamespace=true: the namespace acm-policies already exists with the managed-by label.

Replicated policies

When ACM propagates a policy, it creates a copy in the namespace of every managed cluster on the hub, the replicated policy. Argo CD could treat these copies as extraneous resources of the Application and show it as OutOfSync or even try to delete them. ACM prevents that: it automatically sets the annotation argocd.argoproj.io/compare-options: IgnoreExtraneous on every replicated policy.

Pattern B: a policy bootstraps Argo CD

The bootstrap question from Ep.18: who installs Argo CD on a new cluster? With ACM, the answer is a policy. As soon as a cluster is imported and matches the Placement of the policy, the policy installs OpenShift GitOps and creates a root Application that points to the cluster’s folder in Git. From there, Argo CD configures the rest.

Bootstrap policy: the templates are applied in order, then the local Argo CD takes over

We extend our repository with:

acm-policies/
└── input
    └── gitops-bootstrap
        ├── 01-namespace.yaml          # openshift-gitops-operator
        ├── 02-operatorpolicy.yaml     # OpenShift GitOps Operator
        ├── 03-controller-rbac.yaml    # rights for the local controller
        ├── 04-repo-credentials.yaml   # Git credentials, copied from the hub
        └── 05-root-application.yaml   # app-of-apps for this cluster

The first file creates the namespace for the Operator. The OperatorPolicy in the next step expects it to exist:

input/gitops-bootstrap/01-namespace.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: openshift-gitops-operator
input/gitops-bootstrap/02-operatorpolicy.yaml
apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta1
kind: OperatorPolicy (1)
metadata:
  name: openshift-gitops-operator
spec:
  remediationAction: enforce
  severity: high
  complianceType: musthave
  subscription:
    name: openshift-gitops-operator
    namespace: openshift-gitops-operator
    channel: gitops-1.22 (2)
    source: redhat-operators
    sourceNamespace: openshift-marketplace
  upgradeApproval: Automatic
1 The PolicyGenerator adds OperatorPolicy manifests unchanged as a policy template, no extra wrapping.
2 Pin the channel. Moving to the next version is a one-line pull request.

The root Application is the app-of-apps that contains the Application for every cluster.

input/gitops-bootstrap/05-root-application.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: root
  namespace: openshift-gitops
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/tjungbauer/openshift-clusterconfig-gitops.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: '{{hub printf "clusters/%s/bootstrap" .ManagedClusterName hub}}' (1)
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: false (2)
      selfHeal: true
1 A hub template, resolved on the hub for every cluster: sno gets clusters/sno/bootstrap.
2 Never prune on the root Application. A broken path would otherwise remove everything below it.

The local Argo CD must be allowed to create whatever the root Application brings in. 03-controller-rbac.yaml grants its application-controller cluster-admin rights, the same as in the pull model of Ep.19:

input/gitops-bootstrap/03-controller-rbac.yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: argo-admin
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: openshift-gitops-argocd-application-controller (1)
    namespace: openshift-gitops
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: cluster-admin (2)
1 The service account of the default instance openshift-gitops, which the Operator creates after the installation.
2 Simple and usually fine for platform configuration. For application teams, prefer namespaces labelled with argocd.argoproj.io/managed-by.

And the generator configuration ties it together:

policy-generator.yaml (excerpt)
policies:
  - name: gitops-bootstrap
    remediationAction: enforce
    orderManifests: true (1)
    consolidateManifests: false
    placement:
      labelSelector:
        matchExpressions:
          - key: name (2)
            operator: In
            values:
              - sno
              - bm
    manifests:
      - path: input/gitops-bootstrap/01-namespace.yaml
      - path: input/gitops-bootstrap/02-operatorpolicy.yaml
      - path: input/gitops-bootstrap/03-controller-rbac.yaml
      - path: input/gitops-bootstrap/04-repo-credentials.yaml
      - path: input/gitops-bootstrap/05-root-application.yaml
1 The order matters: the Application CRD only exists after the operator is installed. With orderManifests, the root Application is only created when the operator policy is compliant.
2 The same selection as for the other policies: the clusters sno and bm, selected by the name label that ACM sets on every ManagedCluster. In a larger fleet, a dedicated label such as gitops=enabled makes the bootstrap an opt-in per cluster.
Pattern B is meant for clusters that get their Argo CD from this policy. If you followed the pull or agent part of Ep.19, the GitOps add-on of ACM has already installed OpenShift GitOps on sno and bm, and the policy and the add-on would then manage the same operator. Decide which of the two owns the operator before you enforce this policy, or test Pattern B on a cluster without the add-on.

Who owns what afterwards? The policy owns exactly five objects: the namespace, the operator, the ClusterRoleBinding, the repository secret and the root Application. Everything the root Application brings in belongs to Argo CD. Keep it that way: if you also manage the OpenShift GitOps Subscription with Argo CD on the spoke, the two will fight.

The result in ACM & Argo CD

Once Argo CD has synced the repository, the policies show up in the ACM console under Governance.

The list of Policies shows the three policies of this article in the namespace acm-policies: service-mesh, no-kubeadmin and gitops-bootstrap. For each policy you see the remediation action (inform or enforce), the cluster violations and the policy set, if there is one.

Figure 1. Policies in the namespace acm-policies

A click on a policy opens the details. The Details tab shows the policy templates, here the ConfigurationPolicies and the OperatorPolicy that the PolicyGenerator created from the plain manifests, and the Placement with the selected clusters sno and bm.

The no-kubeadmin policy is a good example for inform: ACM only reports that the secret kubeadmin still exists, it does not delete it.

Figure 2. Results of the policy no-kubeadmin

In the Argo CD UI we can also verify the status (including the resource tree).

The Application acm-policies shows the status Degraded. This is because the policy no-kubeadmin is non-compliant …​ the secrets are still present.

Figure 3. Application acm-policies in Argo CD

The resource tree proves this:

Figure 4. Resource tree of the application acm-policies

Summary

That concludes the mini-series. ACM decides where and checks compliance, Argo CD decides what and keeps it in sync, and Git is the only place where changes are made.

And as always: If it is not in Git, it does not exist. That includes your ACM policies.

item.title: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and how to use it
item.dc:creator: Articles by Thomas Jungbauer
item.description: Enforce mandatory ownership labels on OpenShift namespaces with a CEL ValidatingAdmissionPolicy—and block removal of those labels after creation.
item.content:encoded:
In my last article about the Compliance Operator, Compliance Operator: Writing Your Own Checks with CEL and CustomRules, we discussed CustomRule and how they can enhance the Compliance Operator. CustomRules are good for defining your own policies, for example to check whether a namespace is created with the correct labels. But they cannot stop someone from changing something on the cluster.

The Compliance Operator can detect violations, but it cannot prevent them. This is where ValidatingAdmissionPolicy comes in. It is a native Kubernetes feature that runs directly inside the kube-apiserver. It uses the same language as the CustomRules, CEL, and it can be used to prevent violations from happening in the first place.

Introduction

In this article we will write a policy that:

  • rejects the creation of an application namespace without the mandatory labels example.com/owner and example.com/cost-centre,

  • rejects removing these labels (or setting them to an empty value),

  • ignores platform namespaces, or, in a second variant, only applies to namespaces that follow a naming convention.

The list of excluded platform namespaces is the same as in the Compliance Operator article. This is important: the admission policy and the CustomRule must look at the same set of namespaces, otherwise one of them reports something the other one ignores.

Why a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy?

For a long time, admission control meant writing your own webhook or installing a policy engine such as Gatekeeper or Kyverno. Both are fine tools and worth checking out, but for a simple rule like ours they bring a lot of moving parts that we can avoid if we do not need them.

A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (VAP) is evaluated inside the kube-apiserver. The API admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1 is available since Kubernetes 1.30, which means OpenShift 4.17 and later. A VAP consists of two objects:

ValidatingAdmissionPolicy

What is checked: which requests are matched and which CEL expressions must be true.

ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding

Where and how the policy is enforced (bound to): which namespaces or objects it applies to and what happens on a violation (Deny, Warn, Audit).

If you have followed the Compliance Operator article, the CEL expressions below will look familiar. The difference: a CustomRule evaluates a list of objects on a schedule; a VAP evaluates one object at the moment it is created or changed.

Prerequisites

  • OpenShift 4.17 or newer with cluster-admin permissions.

Designing the Policy

Before writing any YAML, three design decisions have to be made. At the end they will define the policy and its behaviour:

  1. What exactly is forbidden on UPDATE?

  2. Which namespaces are affected?

  3. How to roll it out?

Decision 1: What exactly is forbidden on UPDATE?

This is an important decision and it hit me hard during my tests. The initial approach would be: "every namespace must always have the labels", checked on CREATE and UPDATE. This is a TRAP.

Kubernetes clusters already contain namespaces without these labels. Controllers and operators update namespaces all the time; for example OpenShift synchronises the Pod Security labels and sets the annotations for the SCC UID ranges. If we enforced the labels on every UPDATE, we would eventually break the platform.

Therefore the policy must treat the two operations CREATE and UPDATE differently:

Operation Rule

CREATE

All required labels must be present with a non-empty value. If the labels are missing, the request is rejected.

UPDATE

A required label that was set before (non-empty) must not be removed or emptied. However, changing the value, for example when the ownership moves to another team, is allowed. Updates of old namespaces that never had the labels are allowed as well. If the label is removed or emptied, the request is rejected.

Decision 2: Which namespaces are affected?

Typically, there are two approaches:

Variant A: exclude platform namespaces

Everything is checked except the platform namespaces. This was used in the Compliance Operator article: everything that starts with openshift or kube-, the namespace default, plus additional namespaces that are used by the platform. Adapt the list to whatever runs on your clusters. This is a good approach, but requires you to maintain the list of namespaces that are excluded.

Variant B: namespaces with a naming convention

Only namespaces that follow a convention, for example app-<name>, are checked. Everything else, such as sandboxes or personal projects, is left alone. This is a good approach as well, but requires you to enforce the naming convention when namespaces are created.

Decision 3: How to roll it out?

A policy on namespaces affects everybody, including cluster administrators, GitOps tools and the OpenShift project request template. Therefore we start in Warn/Audit mode and switch to Deny once we know that nothing breaks. I mean, it is always good practice to test first :)

Step 1: The ValidatingAdmissionPolicy

Create the following file 01-vap-namespace-ownership-labels.yaml. It will check for the existence of the required labels on CREATE and UPDATE requests. Such rules are typically built like this:

  1. matchConstraints: decide which requests are matched.

  2. matchConditions: decide which namespaces are affected or not affected.

  3. variables: define the labels that are required.

  4. validations: define the rules that are checked.

01-vap-namespace-ownership-labels.yaml
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: namespace-ownership-labels
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail (1)
  matchConstraints: (2)
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
        resources: ["namespaces"]
  matchConditions: (3)
    - name: exclude-platform-namespaces
      expression: >-
        !object.metadata.name.matches('^(openshift.*|kube-.*|open-cluster-management.*|cert-manager.*|stackrox.*|rhacs-.*|default)$')
  variables:
    - name: requiredLabels (4)
      expression: >-
        ['example.com/owner', 'example.com/cost-centre']
    - name: missingLabels (5)
      expression: >-
        variables.requiredLabels.filter(key,
          !has(object.metadata.labels) ||
          !(key in object.metadata.labels) ||
          object.metadata.labels[key] == '')
    - name: removedLabels (6)
      expression: >-
        request.operation != 'UPDATE' || !has(oldObject.metadata.labels) ? [] :
        variables.missingLabels.filter(key,
          key in oldObject.metadata.labels &&
          oldObject.metadata.labels[key] != '')
  validations:
    - expression: >- (7)
        request.operation != 'CREATE' || size(variables.missingLabels) == 0
      messageExpression: >- (8)
        'Namespace ' + object.metadata.name + ' must carry the label(s) ' +
        variables.missingLabels.join(', ') + ' with a non-empty value.'
      reason: Invalid
    - expression: >- (9)
        size(variables.removedLabels) == 0
      messageExpression: >-
        'The label(s) ' + variables.removedLabels.join(', ') +
        ' must not be removed from namespace ' + object.metadata.name +
        ' or set to an empty value.'
      reason: Forbidden
1 failurePolicy: Fail rejects the request if the expression cannot be evaluated. The other option is Ignore. For a required policy that must always be applied this is the right choice.
2 The policy matches CREATE and UPDATE requests for namespaces. DELETE is not matched, so namespaces can still be removed.
3 matchConditions decide whether the policy applies to a request at all. Here, the platform namespaces are skipped (Variant A). The regular expression is the same as in the CustomRules. Do not forget the anchors ^ and $: without them matches() searches for a substring.
4 variables define the labels that are required. requiredLabels is the single place where the label keys are defined.
5 missingLabels is the list of required labels that are missing or empty in the new object.
6 removedLabels is the list of labels that are missing now but were set (non-empty) in oldObject. For CREATE requests there is no oldObject.
7 Validation for CREATE: nothing may be missing.
8 messageExpression gives feedback to the user and tells which labels are the problem.
9 Validation for UPDATE: nothing that existed may be removed.
The exclusion regex now lives in three places: the CEL expression of the CustomRule and in its instructions, and this policy. When you change one of them, change all three.

Step 2: The Binding

As a second step we need to bind the policy to the namespaces that are affected (all). For the first test we only warn and write audit events. Create the file 02-vapbinding-namespace-ownership-labels.yaml:

02-vapbinding-namespace-ownership-labels.yaml
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
  name: namespace-ownership-labels
spec:
  policyName: namespace-ownership-labels (1)
  validationActions: ["Warn", "Audit"] (2)
1 Reference to the name of the policy.
2 validationActions tells Kubernetes what to do on a violation: Warn returns a warning to the client, Audit adds the violation to the API audit log. The other option is Deny.

Step 3: Apply the Policy and initial test

Apply both objects:

oc apply -f 01-vap-namespace-ownership-labels.yaml
oc apply -f 02-vapbinding-namespace-ownership-labels.yaml

and check that the API server has accepted the expressions.

oc get validatingadmissionpolicy namespace-ownership-labels -o jsonpath='{.status}{"\n"}'

In Warn mode, creating a namespace without labels still works, but oc shows a warning:

oc create namespace app-warn
Warning: Validation failed for ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'namespace-ownership-labels' with binding 'namespace-ownership-labels': Namespace app-warn must carry the label(s) example.com/owner, example.com/cost-centre with a non-empty value.
namespace/app-warn created

Leave the policy in this mode for a while. Watch the output of your GitOps tools and pipelines as well as the audit log, and fix whoever creates namespaces without labels.

Step 4: Switch to Deny

Once you are confident, switch the binding to Deny:

oc patch validatingadmissionpolicybinding namespace-ownership-labels --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"validationActions":["Deny"]}}'
Do not combine Deny and Warn in one binding. Deny already returns the message to the client, Warn would only duplicate it.

Step 5: Test the Policy

Now let us run some detailed tests. We want to make sure that our policy works and that it does not disrupt any platform namespaces or controllers.

Create a namespace without labels. This is rejected, and the message lists the missing labels:

oc create namespace team-a
The namespaces "team-a" is invalid: : ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'namespace-ownership-labels' with binding 'namespace-ownership-labels' denied request: Namespace team-a must carry the label(s) example.com/owner, example.com/cost-centre with a non-empty value.

Create a namespace without labels via the UI. This is rejected as well, and the message is shown directly as feedback to the user.

Create a namespace with only one of the labels. This is rejected as well, and this time only example.com/cost-centre is mentioned:

cat <<'EOF' | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: team-a
  labels:
    example.com/owner: payments
EOF
The namespaces "team-a" is invalid: : ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'namespace-ownership-labels' with binding 'namespace-ownership-labels' denied request: Namespace team-a must carry the label(s) example.com/cost-centre with a non-empty value.

Create the namespace with both labels. This works — yay:

cat <<'EOF' | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: team-a
  labels:
    example.com/owner: payments
    example.com/cost-centre: CC-4711
EOF

Remove a label or set it to an empty value. Both are rejected:

oc label namespace team-a example.com/owner-
oc label namespace team-a example.com/owner= --overwrite
Error from server (Forbidden): namespaces "team-a" is forbidden: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'namespace-ownership-labels' with binding 'namespace-ownership-labels' denied request: The label(s) example.com/owner must not be removed from namespace team-a or set to an empty value.

Change the value of a label, or add an annotation. Both are allowed:

oc label namespace team-a example.com/owner=shop --overwrite
oc annotate namespace team-a example.com/comment=hello

Platform namespaces are not affected:

oc create namespace openshift-demo

Old namespaces that were created before the policy existed can still be updated. Once a label has been added, it is protected as well. Here legacy-app stands for any namespace that existed before the policy:

oc annotate namespace legacy-app example.com/comment=hello      # allowed
oc label namespace legacy-app example.com/owner=legacy          # allowed
oc label namespace legacy-app example.com/owner-                # rejected

Clean up:

oc delete namespace team-a openshift-demo app-warn

What if I need an emergency exit?

The policy above also applies to cluster administrators. Unlike RBAC, admission policies cannot be bypassed with cluster-admin. The labels are protected against accidents, no matter who makes the change.

If you need an emergency exit, you have to build it into the policy yourself, for example with an additional matchCondition on request.userInfo.username for the break-glass account from the cluster-admin allow-list of the previous article.

On purpose I did not build this into the policy, because I think it is a bad idea to have an emergency exit in the policy. If you need namespaces without such labels, add dummy labels that indicate that the namespace is not an application namespace. At least that’s my opinion :)

Variant B: Only Namespaces Following a Naming Convention

Many organisations use a naming convention to distinguish "real" application namespaces from sandboxes or personal projects, for example app-<name> and sandbox-<name>. In that case, copy the policy from Step 1 to 01-vap-namespace-ownership-labels-naming.yaml and replace the matchConditions:

  matchConditions:
    - name: only-application-namespaces
      expression: >-
        object.metadata.name.matches('^app-[a-z0-9-]+$')

We only move from an exclude list to an include list. Everything else stays the same. To test it, we create the following namespaces:

Namespace Labels Result

sandbox-test

none

allowed (does not follow the convention)

application

none

allowed (does not start with app-)

app-shop

none

rejected

app-shop

both

allowed; removing a label afterwards is rejected
Use one of the two variants only. Both policies have the same name, so applying one replaces the other.
If you use the naming convention, adapt the filter() of the CustomRules from the previous article in the same way, for example .filter(ns, ns.metadata.name.matches('^app-[a-z0-9-]+$')). Otherwise the Compliance Operator reports namespaces that the admission policy deliberately ignores.

OpenShift Specifics: Self-Service Projects

On OpenShift, users usually do not create namespaces directly. They run oc new-project, which creates a ProjectRequest. The OpenShift API server then processes the project template and creates the project with its own privileged client. The resulting namespace passes the same admission chain, and therefore the same policy.

A project request cannot pass arbitrary labels. As a consequence, with Variant A in Deny mode, self-service project requests are rejected. You have the following options:

  1. Disable self-provisioning (Recommended) and create application namespaces only through your onboarding process (GitOps, a pipeline, a service catalogue). This is what most regulated customers do anyway. Remove the subjects from the cluster role binding self-provisioners and prevent the API server from restoring them:

    oc patch clusterrolebinding.rbac self-provisioners -p '{"subjects": null}'
oc patch clusterrolebinding.rbac self-provisioners \
  -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"rbac.authorization.kubernetes.io/autoupdate":"false"}}}'

  2. Use Variant B. Self-service projects that do not follow the naming convention (for example sandbox-) are still possible, while app- namespaces must be created with labels through the official process.

  3. Set labels in the project template. Labels defined on the Project object of the template end up on the namespace. However, the template only knows a few parameters, such as the project name and the requesting user, so it cannot fill in a meaningful cost centre. A static value such as unassigned would satisfy the policy, but not the auditor.

Summary

With the two objects ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding, the kube-apiserver itself makes sure that every new application namespace is created with its ownership labels and that nobody removes them by accident. No webhook, no additional operator, no extra pods everything here is native Kubernetes. Together with the CustomRule from the previous article, you now have both sides: prevention at admission time and detection on a schedule, with evidence for the auditor.

The same idea works for the other two guardrails of the previous article. A VAP on ClusterRoleBindings could reject new cluster-admin bindings for identities that are not on the allow-list. Whether this is a good idea depends on how many operators in your cluster create such bindings themselves, so I highly recommend to start in Warn mode there as well.

Thank You

This article would not exist without Max Thüringer and Steffen Lützenkirchen. After listening to the talk "More than just Compliance" at OpenShift User Conference in Vienna, I wanted to see how far the CEL scanner of the Compliance Operator can go.

Thank you, Max Thüringer and Steffen Lützenkirchen, for sharing your ideas and for the inspiration.

References

  • Kubernetes Documentation: Validating Admission Policy

item.title: Compliance Operator: Writing Your Own Checks with CEL and CustomRules
item.dc:creator: Articles by Thomas Jungbauer
item.description: Turn organisation-specific audit requirements into automated checks with the CEL scanner and the CustomRule resource of the OpenShift Compliance Operator.
item.content:encoded:
Five years ago I first tested and described how to achieve compliance for a Kubernetes cluster in my article Compliance Operator. Many years passed since then, but up to this day the Compliance Operator is still one of the most important tools I recommend to my customers and one of the first that is installed on a new cluster. Since the first release of the Operator, it has been constantly improved and extended, for example by adding your own guardrails to the cluster to make sure that the cluster is compliant with your organisation’s requirements.

Today I would like to show you how to write your own checks with the CEL scanner and the CustomRule resource.

Introduction

The Compliance Operator does a great job when it comes to industry benchmarks such as CIS, NIST 800-53, PCI-DSS or BSI. The idea described at Compliance Operator still works today. You define or select a profile and a time of scanning and the operator does the rest for you. Sooner or later, however, every auditor asks a question that is not part of any benchmark because it is individual for each organisation.

For example: "Who owns this namespace?", "Show me that every application is isolated on the network by default." or "Who exactly is cluster-admin, and why?" Until now, the answer usually was a shell script, an automation playbook, a screenshot or a check mark in a spreadsheet. With the CEL scanner and the CustomRule resource, the Compliance Operator can finally check such organisation-specific requirements itself — scheduled, repeatable and with results in the same place as all other compliance checks. All of this defined declaratively, so you can easily integrate it into your GitOps pipeline.

In this article I will build a small but real-world examples: three custom checks that act as platform guardrails. Two of them look at application namespaces, the third one audits who holds cluster-admin. This will extend the standard profile of the Compliance Operator and make it more useful for your organisation.

Once you have the rules in place, you can add them to a TailoredProfile so they become part of your compliance assessment.

The idea is to build the three rules and then add them to a TailoredProfile to make them part of your compliance assessment. If you just need one of the rules, simply remove the other two from the profile.

A Bit of History: CEL in the Compliance Operator

The Compliance Operator traditionally uses OpenSCAP to evaluate its rules. The content (XCCDF / OVAL) is generated by the ComplianceAsCode1 project and shipped with the operator. Writing your own rules in that format is possible, but let us be honest: nobody enjoys building their own content image just to check a label.

The Common Expression Language (CEL) changes this. CEL is a small, side-effect free expression language. If you have ever written a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, you already know it. The integration into the Compliance Operator was finally globally available in version 1.10.0.

CEL does not replace the existing XCCDF profiles. It extends them. Your CIS or PCI-DSS scans continue to work exactly as before.

The Use Case: Platform Guardrails

Many customers have some kind of "platform contract". It is written down in a Confluence page, and it is usually not checked by anybody. Three requirements appear in nearly all of them:

  1. Ownership: every application namespace carries labels that tell who owns it and who pays for it. That is the asset inventory an auditor asks for.

  2. Network segmentation by default: every application namespace contains a default-deny NetworkPolicy for incoming traffic. Applications then explicitly allow what they need.

  3. Privileged access: only an approved list of identities is bound to the ClusterRole cluster-admin. The platform’s own service accounts are allowed, of course, but personal accounts or application service accounts are not.

Why are these good candidates for a CustomRule?

  • The label keys and the list of administrators are specific to each organisation. The operator cannot ship a generic rule for them.

  • The built-in CIS rule ocp4-configure-network-policies-namespaces only verifies that a namespace has at least one NetworkPolicy. A single policy that allows everything would pass. We want a real check: we want the deny-baseline.

  • All three checks only need information from the Kubernetes API. This is exactly what CustomRules are designed for.

CustomRules evaluate Kubernetes/OpenShift API resources only. They cannot inspect files or processes on the nodes. For node-level checks you still use the shipped node profiles, such as ocp4-cis-node.

Prerequisites

  • An OpenShift cluster with cluster-admin permissions.

  • The Compliance Operator 1.10.0 or newer installed in the namespace openshift-compliance. Version 1.8.0 and 1.9.x work as well, but the feature is Technology Preview there.

  • The command line tools oc and jq.

If the operator is not installed yet, have a look at my older articles:

  • Compliance Operator for the manual way, or

  • [Ep.5] Setup & Configure Compliance Operator for the GitOps way.

Verify the installed version:

oc get csv -n openshift-compliance

How a CustomRule Works

Before we write our own rules, let us look at the anatomy of a CustomRule. Such YAML files can get large and messy, but the most important parts are expression and inputs:

CustomRule YAML
apiVersion: compliance.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: CustomRule
metadata:
  name: my-rule
  namespace: openshift-compliance (1)
spec:
  id: my_rule (2)
  title: A short title
  severity: medium (3)
  checkType: Platform (4)
  scannerType: CEL (5)
  inputs: (6)
    - name: pods
      kubernetesInputSpec:
        apiVersion: v1
        resource: pods
  expression: |- (7)
    pods.items.all(p, has(p.spec.securityContext))
  failureReason: Text shown when the check fails (8)
  instructions: How to find and fix the problem (9)
1 CustomRules live in the namespace of the operator.
2 The ID becomes part of the name of the ComplianceCheckResult (underscores are automatically converted to dashes).
3 Can be one of info, low, medium, high (default is medium).
4 CustomRules only support Platform.
5 Must be CEL.
6 The Kubernetes resources the rule needs. Each input becomes a variable in the expression. Without resourceName you get a list object, so the actual objects are found in .items. With resourceNamespace you can limit the query to one namespace.
7 The CEL expression. It must return true when the cluster is compliant.
8 The failureReason is added to the warnings of the ComplianceCheckResult if the check fails.
9 instructions (as well as description and rationale) are copied into the ComplianceCheckResult. Use them to tell the reader how to find the offending objects.
The operator reads the inputs with the ServiceAccount api-resource-collector. This account is basically a cluster-reader, so namespaces, NetworkPolicies, pods, RBAC objects etc. can be read without any additional configuration. If your rule needs resources of an operator (for example HyperConverged of OpenShift Virtualization), you must grant read access to this ServiceAccount yourself.
A CustomRule produces one result for the whole rule, not one result per object. If one namespace out of 200 violates the policy, the rule fails. That is why the instructions field should always contain a command that lists the offending objects.

Step 1: The Ownership Rule

The first rule, that I would like to build, verifies that every application namespace has the labels example.com/owner and example.com/cost-centre with a non-empty value. Our auditor wants to know who owns the namespace and who pays for it.

Platform namespaces must be excluded, otherwise the rule would fail immediately as they do no not have such labels. A regular expression for this: everything that starts with openshift or kube-, plus the namespace default is ignored. In addition, I have also added the namespaces open-cluster-management, stackrox and rhacs- to the exclusion list, these are namespace for Advanced Cluster Management and Advanced Cluster Security respectively and at least on my own demo cluster they exist.

Do not worry about the following YAML. It looks huge, but most of it is just comments. The important parts are the expression field and the inputs section: they define what to check and where.
01-customrule-namespace-ownership-labels.yaml
apiVersion: compliance.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: CustomRule
metadata:
  name: namespace-ownership-labels
  namespace: openshift-compliance
  annotations:
    example.com/controls: "Nist Rule 1.2.3.4" (1)
spec:
  id: namespace_ownership_labels
  title: Application namespaces must have ownership labels set (2)
  severity: medium (3)
  checkType: Platform
  scannerType: CEL
  inputs:
    - name: namespaces (4)
      kubernetesInputSpec:
        apiVersion: v1
        resource: namespaces
  expression: |- (5)
    namespaces.items
      .filter(ns, !ns.metadata.name.matches('^(openshift.*|kube-.*|open-cluster-management.*|cert-manager.*|stackrox.*|rhacs-.*|default)$'))
      .all(ns,
        has(ns.metadata.labels) &&
        ['example.com/owner', 'example.com/cost-centre'].all(key,
          key in ns.metadata.labels && ns.metadata.labels[key] != ''
        )
      )
  description: |- (6)
    Every application namespace must have the labels 'example.com/owner'
    and 'example.com/cost-centre' with a non-empty value set. Platform namespaces (openshift*, kube-*, default)
    are excluded.
  rationale: |- (7)
    Auditors expect an up-to-date inventory of system components and a named
    owner for each of them.
  failureReason: |- (8)
    At least one application namespace is missing the label
    'example.com/owner' or 'example.com/cost-centre' (or the value is empty).
    Run the command from the instructions of this check to list the
    offending namespaces and label them, for example:
    oc label namespace <name> example.com/owner=<team> example.com/cost-centre=<id>
  instructions: |- (9)
    List all application namespaces without complete ownership labels:
    oc get namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[]
      | select(.metadata.name | test("^(openshift.*|kube-.*|open-cluster-management.*|cert-manager.*|stackrox.*|rhacs-.*|default)$") | not)
      | select((.metadata.labels["example.com/owner"] // "") == ""
            or (.metadata.labels["example.com/cost-centre"] // "") == "")
      | .metadata.name'
1 Optional: map the rule to your control framework.
2 The title of the rule.
3 The severity of the rule. Can be one of info, low, medium, high (default is medium).
4 The input section defines the WHERE of the check. The resource namespaces contains the list of all namespaces.
5 The expression field reads like a sentence:

  • filter(…​) removes all platform namespaces. matches() uses RE2 syntax. Note the anchors ^ and $: without them matches() searches for a substring.

  • all(…​) returns true only if the condition is true for every of the remaining namespaces.

  • has(ns.metadata.labels) protects against namespaces without any label. On a real cluster this does not happen, since Kubernetes always sets kubernetes.io/metadata.name, but it costs nothing.

  • The inner all() iterates over the list of mandatory label keys. key in map checks whether the key exists and that the value is not empty.
6 Detailed description of the rule.
7 Rationale: why are we checking this?
8 The failureReason is added to the warnings of the ComplianceCheckResult if the check fails.
9 The instructions are copied into the ComplianceCheckResult. Use it to tell the reader how to find the offending objects.
This is our first CustomRule object. We will define the other rules in the same way, then apply them all at once.

Step 2: The Default-Deny Rule

The second rule is more interesting because it combines two inputs:

  • the list of namespaces and

  • the list of all NetworkPolicies.

For every application namespace there must exist at least one NetworkPolicy that:

  • lives in that namespace,

  • selects all pods (empty podSelector),

  • covers the policy type Ingress and

  • does not define any ingress rule, which means: nothing is allowed.

In short, every application namespace must have a deny-all NetworkPolicy for ingress.

Create the file 02-customrule-namespace-default-deny-ingress.yaml:

02-customrule-namespace-default-deny-ingress.yaml
apiVersion: compliance.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: CustomRule
metadata:
  name: namespace-default-deny-ingress
  namespace: openshift-compliance
  annotations:
    example.com/controls: "Nist Rule 1.2.3.4"
spec:
  id: namespace_default_deny_ingress
  title: Application namespaces have a default-deny ingress NetworkPolicy
  description: |-
    Every application namespace must contain a NetworkPolicy that selects
    all pods (empty podSelector), covers the policy type 'Ingress' and
    defines no ingress rules.
    Additional allow policies are expected on top of it. Platform namespaces
    (openshift*, kube-*, default) are excluded.
  rationale: |-
    Without a default-deny baseline every pod accepts traffic from every
    other pod in the cluster.
  severity: high
  checkType: Platform
  scannerType: CEL
  inputs:
    - name: namespaces
      kubernetesInputSpec:
        apiVersion: v1
        resource: namespaces
    - name: networkpolicies (1)
      kubernetesInputSpec:
        apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 (2)
        resource: networkpolicies
  expression: |-
    namespaces.items
      .filter(ns, !ns.metadata.name.matches('^(openshift.*|kube-.*|open-cluster-management.*|cert-manager.*|stackrox.*|rhacs-.*|default)$'))
      .all(ns,
        networkpolicies.items.exists(np,
          np.metadata.namespace == ns.metadata.name &&
          (!has(np.spec.podSelector.matchLabels) || size(np.spec.podSelector.matchLabels) == 0) &&
          (!has(np.spec.podSelector.matchExpressions) || size(np.spec.podSelector.matchExpressions) == 0) &&
          (!has(np.spec.policyTypes) || 'Ingress' in np.spec.policyTypes) &&
          (!has(np.spec.ingress) || size(np.spec.ingress) == 0)
        )
      )
  failureReason: |-
    At least one application namespace has no default-deny ingress
    NetworkPolicy (empty podSelector, policyType Ingress, no ingress rules).
    Run the command from the instructions of this check to list the
    offending namespaces and add a default-deny policy to each of them.
  instructions: |-
    Lists every application namespace that has no default-deny ingress policy.
    A policy counts as default-deny if it selects all pods, covers Ingress and
    allows nothing. Copy the lines below into a bash shell:

    for ns in $(oc get namespaces -o name | cut -d/ -f2 \
        | grep -Ev '^(openshift.*|kube-.*|open-cluster-management.*|cert-manager.*|stackrox.*|rhacs-.*|default)$'); do
      oc get networkpolicies -n "$ns" -o json | jq -e '.items[] | select(
          (.spec.podSelector.matchLabels      // {} | length) == 0 and
          (.spec.podSelector.matchExpressions // [] | length) == 0 and
          (.spec.policyTypes // ["Ingress"] | index("Ingress")) and
          (.spec.ingress // [] | length) == 0
        )' > /dev/null || echo "missing default-deny: $ns"
    done
1 A second input. NetworkPolicies are namespace-scoped; since no resourceNamespace is set, the policies of all namespaces are fetched.
2 For resources outside the core API group, group and version are written together, exactly like the apiVersion in a manifest.

Some details of the expression field are worth a second look:

  • filter(…​) removes all platform namespaces that matches()

  • all(…​) returns true only if the condition is true for every of the remaining namespaces.

  • a network policy object must exist that:

    • lives in that namespace,

    • has an empty podSelector,

    • has not policyTypes set to Ingress,

    • has no ingress rules,

  • Additional allow policies (for example to let the OpenShift router in) are fine. We only require that the deny baseline exists.

This is just an example that shows how to use two inputs in a CustomRule. If you enforce the baseline cluster-wide with a BaselineAdminNetworkPolicy or an AdminNetworkPolicy instead of per-namespace NetworkPolicies, this rule is not the right one for you. In that case write a rule that checks the (cluster-scoped) admin policy instead.

Step 3: The cluster-admin Allow-List

The third rule answers the classic auditor question "Who is cluster-admin?".

The CIS OpenShift Benchmark (control 5.1.1) recommends to restrict the use of cluster-admin, but it cannot know who is allowed in your organisation. That is a perfect job for a CustomRule.

A common mistake is to look only at the ClusterRoleBinding that is called cluster-admin. Any ClusterRoleBinding can reference the ClusterRole cluster-admin, and OpenShift itself ships several of them. Therefore, the rule looks at all ClusterRoleBindings whose roleRef points to cluster-admin, and checks every subject of these bindings.

Before you write the allow-list, look at the current state of your cluster:

oc get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r '.items[]
  | select(.roleRef.kind == "ClusterRole" and .roleRef.name == "cluster-admin")
  | .metadata.name as $crb | .subjects[]?
  | "\($crb)\t\(.kind)\t\(.namespace // "-")\t\(.name)"' | column -t

This selects all ClusterRoleBindings that reference the ClusterRole cluster-admin and lists the subjects of each binding. The output looks like this:

cluster-admin                    Group           -                                   system:masters
cluster-admin-0                  ServiceAccount  openshift-gitops                    openshift-gitops-argocd-application-controller
cluster-admin-crb                Group           -                                   cluster-admin
cluster-admins                   Group           -                                   system:cluster-admins
cluster-admins                   User            -                                   system:admin
cluster-network-operator         ServiceAccount  openshift-network-operator          cluster-network-operator
cluster-storage-operator-role    ServiceAccount  openshift-cluster-storage-operator  cluster-storage-operator
cluster-version-operator         ServiceAccount  openshift-cluster-version           default
...

You will find the platform-internal groups system:masters and system:cluster-admins, the user system:admin and a number of service accounts in openshift-* namespaces that belong to the platform operators. Everything else was added later by someone and deserves a closer look.

The allow-list — the subjects the rule treats as acceptable — has three parts:

Subject kind Allowed

Group

The platform groups system:masters and system:cluster-admins, plus the group of the platform team (here cluster-admin, for example synchronised from LDAP or Entra ID).

User

The platform user system:admin and one named break-glass account. Personal accounts are not allowed. The platform team gets its rights through the group.

ServiceAccount

Every service account in a platform namespace (openshift*, kube-*), plus an explicit list of namespace/name pairs for tools such as a cluster-wide Argo CD instance.

The following file is a full example of a CustomRule that checks the allow-list for cluster-admin. The callouts below walk through every part of the expression.

03-customrule-cluster-admin-allow-list.yaml
apiVersion: compliance.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: CustomRule
metadata:
  name: cluster-admin-allow-list
  namespace: openshift-compliance
  annotations:
    example.com/controls: "Nist Rule 1.2.3.4"
spec:
  id: cluster_admin_allow_list
  title: Only approved identities are allowed to hold cluster-admin privileges
  description: |-
    Every subject of every ClusterRoleBinding that grants cluster-admin
    privileges must be on the organisation's allow-list. A binding grants
    cluster-admin privileges if it references the ClusterRole 'cluster-admin'
    or any other ClusterRole with a wildcard rule ('*' API groups, '*'
    resources, '*' verbs), for example a renamed copy of cluster-admin.
    Allowed are: the platform-internal groups and users of OpenShift,
    service accounts in platform namespaces (openshift*, kube-*), an
    explicitly named break-glass account, explicitly listed service accounts
    and the group of platform administrators - but only if that group exists
    and every member of it is an approved administrator. Everything else, in
    particular personal user accounts, application service accounts and
    broad groups such as 'system:authenticated', fails the check.
  rationale: |-
    cluster-admin grants unrestricted access to every resource in the
    cluster. Privileged access must be limited to a small, documented and
    reviewed set of identities.
  severity: high
  checkType: Platform
  scannerType: CEL
  inputs:
    - name: crbs (1)
      kubernetesInputSpec:
        apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
        resource: clusterrolebindings
    - name: clusterroles (2)
      kubernetesInputSpec:
        apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
        resource: clusterroles
    - name: groups (3)
      kubernetesInputSpec:
        apiVersion: user.openshift.io/v1
        resource: groups
  expression: |-
    // ---- allow-list: might be exported into a ConfigMap ---- (4)
    // ---- every dynamic value is stored in a map ----
    [{
      'platformGroups':         ['system:masters', 'system:cluster-admins'],
      'adminGroups':            ['cluster-admin'],
      'approvedAdmins':         ['alice.admin@example.com', 'bob.admin@example.com'],
      'allowedUsers':           ['system:admin', 'breakglass-admin'],
      'allowedServiceAccounts': ['gitops-system/argocd-application-controller', 'rhacs-operator/rhacs-operator-controller-manager']
    }].all(cfg,
      crbs.items (5)
        .filter(crb,
          crb.roleRef.kind == 'ClusterRole' &&
          has(crb.subjects) && crb.subjects != null &&
          (crb.roleRef.name == 'cluster-admin' || (6)
           clusterroles.items.exists(cr,
             cr.metadata.name == crb.roleRef.name &&
             has(cr.rules) && cr.rules != null &&
             cr.rules.exists(r,
               has(r.apiGroups) && '*' in r.apiGroups &&
               has(r.resources) && '*' in r.resources &&
               '*' in r.verbs))))
        .all(crb, crb.subjects.all(s, (7)
          // groups: built-in groups, or an admin group that exists and has only approved members
          (s.kind == 'Group' && ( (8)
            s.name in cfg.platformGroups ||
            (s.name in cfg.adminGroups &&
             groups.items.exists(g, g.metadata.name == s.name) &&
             groups.items.filter(g, g.metadata.name == s.name).all(g,
               !has(g.users) || g.users == null ||
               g.users.all(u, u in cfg.approvedAdmins)))
          )) ||
          // users: allowed users, or service accounts of platform namespaces written as User
          (s.kind == 'User' && ( (9)
            s.name in cfg.allowedUsers ||
            s.name.matches('^system:serviceaccount:(openshift[^:]*|kube-[^:]*):[^:]+$')
          )) ||
          // service accounts: platform namespaces, or explicitly listed namespace/name pairs
          (s.kind == 'ServiceAccount' && has(s.namespace) && ( (10)
            s.namespace.matches('^(openshift.*|kube-.*)$') ||
            (s.namespace + '/' + s.name) in cfg.allowedServiceAccounts
          ))
        ))
    )
  failureReason: |-
    At least one subject that holds cluster-admin privileges is not on the
    allow-list, or the platform administrator group contains a member that
    is not an approved administrator.
  instructions: |- (11)
    List all subjects with cluster-admin privileges that are not on the
    allow-list:
    jq -rn \
      --slurpfile crbs <(oc get clusterrolebindings -o json) \
      --slurpfile roles <(oc get clusterroles -o json) \
      --slurpfile groups <(oc get groups -o json) '
      # ---- allow-list: edit here ----
      {
        platformGroups:         ["system:masters", "system:cluster-admins"],
        adminGroups:            ["cluster-admin"],
        approvedAdmins:         ["alice.admin@example.com", "bob.admin@example.com"],
        allowedUsers:           ["system:admin", "breakglass-admin"],
        allowedServiceAccounts: ["gitops-system/argocd-application-controller", "rhacs-operator/rhacs-operator-controller-manager"]
      } as $cfg
      | [$roles[0].items[]
          | select(.metadata.name == "cluster-admin" or any(.rules[]?;
              ((.apiGroups // []) | index("*")) and ((.resources // []) | index("*"))
              and ((.verbs // []) | index("*"))))
          | .metadata.name] as $adminRoles
      | $crbs[0].items[]
      | select(.roleRef.kind == "ClusterRole"
          and (.roleRef.name == "cluster-admin" or (.roleRef.name | IN($adminRoles[]))))
      | .metadata.name as $crb | .roleRef.name as $role | .subjects[]? | . as $s
      | select(
          ((.kind == "Group") and ((.name | IN($cfg.platformGroups[]))
             or ((.name | IN($cfg.adminGroups[]))
                 and ([$groups[0].items[] | select(.metadata.name == $s.name)] as $g
                      | ($g | length) > 0
                        and all($g[]; (.users // []) | all(IN($cfg.approvedAdmins[])))))))
          or ((.kind == "User") and ((.name | IN($cfg.allowedUsers[]))
                or (.name | test("^system:serviceaccount:(openshift[^:]*|kube-[^:]*):[^:]+$"))))
          or ((.kind == "ServiceAccount") and (((.namespace // "") | test("^(openshift.*|kube-.*)$"))
                or ((.namespace // "") + "/" + .name | IN($cfg.allowedServiceAccounts[]))))
          | not)
      | "\($crb) -> \($role): \(.kind) \(.namespace // "-")/\(.name)"
        + (if .kind == "Group" then
             ([$groups[0].items[] | select(.metadata.name == $s.name) | (.users // [])[]]
              | if length == 0 then " (no Group object or no members)"
                else " (members: " + join(", ") + ")" end)
           else "" end)'
1 The list of all ClusterRoleBindings.
2 The list of all ClusterRoles. It is used to find roles that are equivalent to cluster-admin.
3 The list of all OpenShift Group objects. It is used to verify the members of the allowed group.
4 A map for the alow list and any dynamic values. Easier to manage than a long list of strings.
5 Selecting the relevant ClusterRoleBindings: kind == ClusterRole, subject exists
6 Role reference name is cluster-admin or any other ClusterRole with a wildcard rule ('' API groups, '' resources, '*' verbs)
7 Subject is a Group OR a User OR a ServiceAccount
8 Group is either a platform group OR an admin group that exists and has only approved admins
9 User is either an allowed user OR a service account of a platform namespace written as User
10 ServiceAccount is either a platform namespace OR an explicitly listed namespace/name pair (here: the Argo CD application controller)
11 Pretty decent command to list the offending bindings.

Some details are important here, and they are the reason why I did not simply allow everything that starts with system::

  • Broad system groups: system:authenticated, system:unauthenticated and system:serviceaccounts:<namespace> are system groups as well. Binding one of them to cluster-admin is about the worst thing you can do to a cluster. A prefix match on system: would happily accept them. Therefore the rule uses an explicit list of groups.

  • Service accounts as User subjects: A service account can also appear as a subject of kind User with the name system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>. The rule treats such subjects like service accounts and only accepts them if the namespace is a platform namespace.

  • Exact namespace/name pairs: For service accounts outside the platform namespaces the rule compares namespace/name. A service account with the same name in another namespace does not pass.

The rule deliberately ignores RoleBindings. A RoleBinding to cluster-admin only grants full access within one namespace. ClusterRoles that grant broad privileges without using //* wildcards are also outside the scope of this example; extend the expression if you need to treat those as equivalent to cluster-admin.

Step 4: Create the Rules and Check Their Status

Apply the three rules:

oc apply -f 01-customrule-namespace-ownership-labels.yaml
oc apply -f 02-customrule-namespace-default-deny-ingress.yaml
oc apply -f 03-customrule-cluster-admin-allow-list.yaml

The operator validates the CEL expression immediately. Only rules in the state Ready can be used in a profile:

oc get customrules -n openshift-compliance
NAME                             STATUS   AGE
cluster-admin-allow-list         Ready    10s
namespace-default-deny-ingress   Ready    12s
namespace-ownership-labels       Ready    14s

If the status is Error, the reason can be found in the status of the object:

oc get customrule namespace-ownership-labels -n openshift-compliance -o jsonpath='{.status.errorMessage}{"\n"}'
Do not use the short name cr. In the Compliance Operator, cr stands for complianceremediations. I fell into that trap more than once.

Step 5: TailoredProfile and ScanSettingBinding

CustomRules are never scanned directly. They must be bundled into a TailoredProfile, which is then bound to a ScanSetting (when to scan) via a ScanSettingBinding (which profile to scan).

Create the file tailoredprofile.yaml:

tailoredprofile.yaml
apiVersion: compliance.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: TailoredProfile
metadata:
  name: platform-guardrails               (1)
  namespace: openshift-compliance
spec:
  title: Platform guardrails
  description: Organisation-specific checks for namespaces and privileged access
  enableRules:
    - kind: CustomRule                    (2)
      name: namespace-ownership-labels
      rationale: Asset inventory and accountability for every namespace
    - kind: CustomRule
      name: namespace-default-deny-ingress
      rationale: Network segmentation as the default for every namespace
    - kind: CustomRule
      name: cluster-admin-allow-list
      rationale: Privileged access limited to approved identities
1 The name of the TailoredProfile becomes the name of the ComplianceScan and the prefix of all results.
2 The kind must be set to CustomRule. Without it, the operator looks for a regular Rule with that name.
A TailoredProfile cannot mix CEL-based checks with the classic OpenSCAP-based Rule objects (such as the CIS rules). CustomRules may only be combined with other CEL rules. Keep your custom checks in their own profile, which is a good idea anyway.

Create the file scansettingbinding.yaml:

scansettingbinding.yaml
apiVersion: compliance.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: ScanSettingBinding
metadata:
  name: platform-guardrails
